{{DISPLAYTITLE:Stating the right thing}}
{{Technical|Lean theorem prover/Foundations/Terms, types and judgments}}
{{Lean theorem prover map}}

Lean checks that a proof proves the statement that was written. It cannot check that the
statement written is the one that was meant. This page shows, with lines Lean accepts, how the
two can come apart, gives a published case in which they did, and says what therefore has to be
read by people.

== What the check covers ==

Pollack divided the belief in a machine-checked proof into two questions: whether the proof is a
correct derivation, which a machine can settle, and whether the theorem means what is claimed,
which it cannot. For the second, nobody has to read the proof. What has to be read is the
statement, the assumptions left standing, and every definition the statement uses, and every
definition those use in turn.<ref name="pollack">R. Pollack, "How to believe a machine-checked proof", in Giovanni Sambin and Jan M. Smith (eds), ''Twenty Five Years of Constructive Type Theory'', Oxford University Press, 1998, chapter 11 (from p. 205); first issued as BRICS Report RS-97-18, Aarhus University, 1997. [https://doi.org/10.7146/brics.v4i18.18945 doi:10.7146/brics.v4i18.18945]</ref>
Lean's own guide to validating proofs says the same of Lean: a statement and all the definitions it
refers to must be examined with care, especially where custom notation or type classes are
involved.<ref name="refval">''The Lean Language Reference'', version for Lean 4.34.0, section "Validating a Lean Proof". [https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/ValidatingProofs/ lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/ValidatingProofs], consulted 14 October 2026.</ref>

That is usually a short text, even when the proof is long. It is also where much of the remaining
risk lies.

== Numbers that are not quite school numbers ==

In Lean every function gives an answer for every input. Subtraction of natural numbers (0, 1, 2,
...) therefore has to give some natural number when the result would be negative, and Lean gives
0. Division by zero also has to give something, and for natural numbers and integers Lean gives 0:

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
#eval (3 - 5 : Nat)
#eval (7 / 0 : Nat)
#eval (7 / 0 : Int)

example : (3 : Nat) - 5 = 0 := rfl
example : (7 : Nat) / 0 = 0 := rfl
</pre>

Lean 4.34.1 prints <code>0</code> three times and accepts both examples.

These are conventions, not contradictions. A FAQ on the subject puts it this way: such a division
is a function that agrees with ordinary division wherever the denominator is not zero, and its
value at zero is simply defined. The theorems that make division useful, such as that a number
divided by itself is 1, carry the hypothesis that the denominator is not zero, so an illegal
division still fails, at the point where one of those theorems is applied.<ref name="xena">The Xena Project (blog), "Division by zero in type theory: a FAQ", 5 July 2020. [https://xenaproject.wordpress.com/2020/07/05/division-by-zero-in-type-theory-a-faq/ xenaproject.wordpress.com/2020/07/05/division-by-zero-in-type-theory-a-faq]</ref>

The convention matters when a statement is written. Someone who means "subtract, then add back"
may write this:

<pre class="lean lean-fails" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
theorem sub_then_add (a b : Nat) : a - b + b = a := by
  omega
</pre>

Lean refuses it, and the automation it was asked to use reports where the statement breaks:

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
error: omega could not prove the goal:
a possible counterexample may satisfy the constraints
  d ≥ 0
  c ≥ 0
  c - d ≥ 1
where
 c := ↑b
 d := ↑a
</pre>

That is, whenever <code>b</code> is larger than <code>a</code>. Here the mistake announced itself.
The dangerous case is the reverse: a statement that is true only because of the convention, which
Lean accepts without comment.

== Hypotheses that cannot all hold ==

A theorem says that if its hypotheses hold, its conclusion does. If the hypotheses can never hold
together, the theorem is true and says nothing:

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
theorem strange (n : Nat) (h1 : n &lt; 2) (h2 : 5 &lt; n) : n = 100 := by
  omega
</pre>

Lean accepts this. No number is both below 2 and above 5, so any conclusion follows. In a long
statement with many hypotheses, such a clash is easy to miss, and a proof of it can look like a
proof of something hard.

A milder fault is a hypothesis that is not contradictory but is not in the original problem
either. It makes the formal problem easier than the one it claims to state.

== Definitions are part of the statement ==

A statement means only what its definitions mean. Here is a definition of a prime number that
forgets one condition, that a prime is at least 2:

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
def IsPrime (n : Nat) : Prop := ∀ d, d ∣ n → d = 1 ∨ d = n

theorem one_is_prime : IsPrime 1 := by
  intro d hd
  left
  exact Nat.dvd_one.mp hd
</pre>

Lean accepts that 1 is prime, correctly, for this definition. Every theorem stated with
<code>IsPrime</code> is a theorem about this definition, not about primes. Pollack's remedy is the
one mathematics already uses: develop shared libraries of formal definitions that are checked, read
and used by many people, so that their definitions come to be trusted as meaning what they
claim.<ref name="pollack" /> In Lean that library is Mathlib (see
[[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/A library of mathematics|a library of mathematics]]).

Notation is part of the statement too. A Lean file can define new notation and new type class
instances, and these change how a statement is read; Lean's guide warns that they can be used to
change what a statement means, and notes that some independent checkers can print a statement
plainly, unaffected by the file's notation.<ref name="refval" />

== A published case ==

miniF2F is a set of 488 problems from mathematics competitions, among them the IMO, AIME and AMC,
and from some textbooks, each stated formally in Lean and used to compare automated provers. A
review posted in 2025 found discrepancies between the formal and the informal statements in
more than half of its problems. In one AIME problem, the formal version carried three hypotheses
that certain expressions are not zero, which the original problem did not state and which made
the proof easier; in another problem a missing pair of brackets made the formal statement wrong
and unprovable. The authors corrected the statements and published a revised set.<ref name="minif2f">Azim Ospanov, Farzan Farnia and Roozbeh Yousefzadeh, "miniF2F-Lean Revisited: Reviewing Limitations and Charting a Path Forward", arXiv:2511.03108, 5 November 2025. [https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.03108 arxiv.org/abs/2511.03108]</ref>
Every one of those statements had been checked by Lean, in the only sense Lean can check them.

== Who reads the statement ==

The statement is the part a person has to read, and Lean's strictest procedure is built around
that fact: the statement to be proved is written separately, in a trusted setting, and the proof is
accepted only if what it proves matches that text exactly. Even then, the guide lists human error
or misleading presentation in that trusted statement among the things that remain.<ref name="refval" />
The project this wiki records says the same in its own words: a proof checker is not a reviewer
(see [[Principia Machina/Lean transition|the move to Lean]]).
